subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
subtype: Approach: pros-and-cons list with a fixed deadline [Thinking]
passage:
My first job as an engineer left me tired and irritable, and for months I kept thinking about it in the shower without getting anywhere. Nilesh, who sits two rows behind me, said, "You're just going around in circles. Put a date on it."

So one Sunday I drew a line down a page. Stay: a good manager, steady pay, decent people, but no learning and a long commute. Leave: new things to learn, but risk, no offer yet, and a pay cut. I chose the first of December, three months off, as my deadline. Until then I would look for facts and stop asking the same question every night.

The list didn't decide anything. But the date let me stop brooding. Karthik

qa.q: How far away was the date Karthik set to decide?
qa.a: Three months off, the first of December.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling before making the list?
qa.a: Karthik felt stuck, tired and irritable, going round in circles without progress.

qa.q: What could Karthik do in the three months to make the final decision better, and why?
qa.a: Karthik could talk to people about other roles and try small learning projects, because facts gathered before the date make the choice less of a guess.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see Karthik's decision to set a date?
qa.a: Nilesh probably feels glad the advice helped, having noticed the circling, and may check in when December approaches.

grounding: An engineer unhappy in a first job lists what is gained and lost by staying or leaving and sets a date three months away to decide.

passage:
Mentor's note, graduate engineer programme, month 5. Written by Gurpreet.
Zeenat asked for extra time in our monthly meeting. She said she has been unhappy at the plant for weeks and keeps going round in circles about leaving.
She had brought two columns on a sheet of paper. Staying: steady team, learning to read the machines, the certification the company pays for next spring. Losing by staying: night shifts, no design work, feeling like a spare pair of hands. Leaving: chance at design roles, a city closer to her parents. Losing by leaving: the certification, a short record on her CV.
She read it aloud, then said, "If I don't give this a date, I'll be thinking about it at forty." She wrote 15 June at the top, three months from now, and circled it.
I agreed to check in monthly, and suggested she add new points to the sheet as they come up rather than deciding early.

qa.q: What date did Zeenat write at the top of the sheet?
qa.a: She wrote 15 June, three months from the meeting.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's line about being forty suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt tired and stuck from circling the question for weeks, and afraid of brooding on it for years without a date.

qa.q: What else could Zeenat try alongside the list before 15 June?
qa.a: She could ask her manager if any design tasks are possible, which would test one of the biggest losses of staying before the deadline arrives.

qa.q: How does Zeenat's plan look to her mentor?
qa.a: The mentor sees a clear, sensible structure and supports it with monthly check-ins, while encouraging her not to decide early.

grounding: Shows an engineer unhappy in a first job listing gains and losses of staying and leaving and setting a decision date three months ahead.

subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
subtype: Approach: pros-and-cons list with a fixed deadline [Thinking]
passage:
Tuesday night.
Spent another lunch break staring at job sites instead of eating. This has been going on since Diwali. Rajni finally said on the phone, "You're either leaving or staying, but you can't keep doing both."
So tonight I did it properly. Left side of the page, staying at the software firm: good salary, kind team lead, visa project coming up. What I lose: I'm testing other people's code, not writing any, and I'm bored by eleven every morning. Right side, leaving: a chance at a real developer role, maybe more learning. What I lose: the visa project, and I'm only eight months in.
Seeing it written, both sides are real. That's why I keep brooding.
So I set a date. 30 April, three months from today. Until then I stop checking job sites daily. On the 30th I read this page again and choose.
Gurpreet

qa.q: What date did Gurpreet set to decide?
qa.a: Gurpreet set 30 April, three months from that night.

qa.q: How has Gurpreet been feeling at work, and what shows it?
qa.a: Gurpreet has been bored and restless, staring at job sites during lunch and feeling bored by eleven every morning.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet do before 30 April to make the choice clearer?
qa.a: Gurpreet could ask the team lead about moving toward writing code, since that would show whether the biggest problem can change without leaving.

qa.q: How might Rajni see Gurpreet's new plan?
qa.a: Rajni, who pushed for a decision, would likely feel relieved that Gurpreet has stopped doing both and set a clear date.

grounding: Shows an engineer in a first job writing the gains and losses of staying and leaving and setting a decision date three months away.
